documents.title: New Patient Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
21 yo woman here to establish. Moved her care to us after her old pediatric/adolescent office stopped seeing adults. Works part time waiting tables in town. No insurance right now; Medicaid application started, she has the confirmation letter.

Asthma: since she was little. Says it is 'bad asthma', has been told severe. Uses albuterol a few days most weeks, more with colds and in the spring. Fluticasone 220 one puff BID is prescribed but she admits she takes it 'when I remember, maybe half the time'. Night cough a couple of nights a month. Has a peak flow meter at home, does not use it much. Never been on a combination inhaler that she knows of.
Allergies: seasonal sneezing, itchy eyes in spring and fall; levocetirizine as needed helps.

PMH: asthma, allergic rhinitis. PSH: none. Meds as listed. NKDA.
FH: mother has asthma. A maternal uncle has eczema.
SH: never smoked, no vaping. Drinks a little on weekends, 1-2.

Exam: well, talking in full sentences. HEENT: nasal turbinates mildly pale and boggy, OP clear. Neck supple, no nodes. Lungs: clear, no wheeze, good air movement. Heart RRR, no murmur. Abd soft. Skin clear.

A/P
1. Severe persistent asthma, partly controlled. The main issue is adherence to the controller. Talked through why the fluticasone matters even on good days, linked it to brushing teeth. Spacer technique reviewed. Refill albuterol and fluticasone. Return 4 mo, sooner if using albuterol more than twice a week.
2. Allergic rhinitis: levocetirizine prn, ok.
3. Health maintenance: hep C screen today with baseline CBC/BMP. Will get vaccine and Pap history from prior office. Flu/COVID/pneumococcal in the fall.
PHQ-2 negative. Request records from prior primary care practice.

documents.title: Hospital discharge summary (received 01/16/2024)
documents.author: hospital medicine
documents.body:
Regional hospital, Department of Medicine
Admission 01/08/2024  Discharge 01/12/2024
Patient: Jada Simmons  DOB 09/08/2001
Allergies: NKDA

Admitting diagnosis: acute asthma exacerbation with hypercapnic respiratory failure

History: 22 yo with lifelong asthma on fluticasone and albuterol, adherence by her report irregular, brought in overnight by EMS with 2 days of worsening wheeze after a cold. Failed to improve with back-to-back nebulizers and IV steroids in the ED and was intubated there.

Hospital course: Admitted to the MICU on the ventilator. Treated with scheduled bronchodilators and IV corticosteroids. Rapid improvement; extubated on hospital day 2 without difficulty. Transferred to the floor, weaned to room air, ambulating without desaturation by discharge. No pneumonia on imaging.

Discharge medications:
- prednisone 40 mg daily x 5 days
- fluticasone propionate HFA 220 mcg 1 puff twice daily (continue)
- albuterol HFA 2 puffs q4-6h prn
- levocetirizine 5 mg daily prn

Instructions: take the controller every day. Follow up with PCP within 1 week.
Discharging physician: hospitalist

documents.title: Post-hospital Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Seen after her admission 1/8-1/12 at the regional hospital, discharge summary reviewed. She was intubated in their ED for a severe asthma flare that started with a cold, extubated the next day. Finished the 5 days of prednisone yesterday. Back at work Saturday. Says she was scared, first time on a breathing machine.

Now: mild cough in the mornings, no night waking this week, albuterol once or twice a day, less each day. Taking fluticasone twice a day since discharge.

Exam: comfortable, full sentences. Lungs clear, no wheeze, normal expiratory phase. Heart regular.

A/P: Severe persistent asthma, recovering after a near-fatal exacerbation needing intubation. Regimen unchanged per discharge plan; long talk about using the controller daily, not just after flares. She has a peak flow meter, encouraged to start using it again. Written instructions on when to go to the ED: albuterol not lasting 4 hours, can't speak full sentences. Recheck 3 months.

documents.title: peak flow
documents.author: patient
documents.body: started doing the peak flow thing again like you said. what number am i supposed to worry about

documents.title: RE: peak flow
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Great that you're using it. For the next 2 weeks, do it each morning when you feel well and write down the best number you get. That becomes your personal best. Bring the log to your April visit and we'll write your zones on your action plan. Until then, the rule is the same: if albuterol isn't lasting 4 hours or you can't talk in full sentences, go to the ED.

Gyn: sees an outside gynecology office for women's health; no contraception from us. LMP 2 weeks ago, regular.

documents.title: Gynecology visit letter (received 12/27/2024)
documents.author: obstetrics and gynecology
documents.body:
Outside OB/GYN group
Visit date: 12/23/2024
Re: Jada Simmons, DOB 09/08/2001
Allergies: NKDA

Dear colleague,

I saw Ms. Simmons for five days of burning with urination, frequency, and a yellow vaginal discharge. Over the past month she has had unprotected intercourse with more than one partner.

Her history includes severe persistent asthma and allergic rhinitis. Medications: albuterol inhaler as needed, fluticasone 220 mcg inhaler twice daily (she tells me she misses doses), levocetirizine as needed. No surgeries.

Vital signs were normal. On speculum exam there was purulent discharge from the cervical os, and bimanual exam elicited cervical motion tenderness. No adnexal mass.

Urine hCG negative. Urinalysis not suggestive of urinary infection. Cervical NAAT came back positive for gonorrhea and negative for chlamydia. HIV antigen/antibody and RPR were both negative.

Impression: gonococcal cervicitis; high-risk sexual exposure.

Plan: ceftriaxone 500 mg IM given in the office, plus doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for seven days started empirically before the chlamydia result returned (she is to finish it). Abstain until treatment complete and partners treated; partner referral information given and the case reported as required. Condom counseling. Return in three months for repeat testing.

Sincerely,
Attending gynecologist

documents.author: obstetrics and gynecology
documents.body:
Outside OB/GYN group
Visit date: 03/24/2025
Re: Jada Simmons, DOB 09/08/2001
Allergies: NKDA

Dear colleague,

Ms. Simmons came back three months after we treated her gonococcal cervicitis, and she brought a new problem: a rash she first noticed about three weeks ago. It started as a handful of faint spots on her chest and back and has spread to her arms, legs, palms and soles. It does not itch or hurt and has looked the same throughout. No fever, sore throat, tiredness, joint pain or recent illness. No new medicines, foods or supplements. No genital sores, discharge or urinary symptoms now. No change in vision, no headaches, no neurologic complaints. She continues to have several male partners and uses condoms some of the time.

Medications unchanged: albuterol as needed, fluticasone 220 mcg twice daily, levocetirizine as needed.

T 36.9 C, BP 112/72, HR 82. She looks well. Skin: symmetric, faintly red macules and papules over the chest, back, abdomen, arms, legs, palms and soles; not scaly, no vesicles, do not blanch. No lymph node enlargement, no liver or spleen enlargement, mouth and genital mucosa clear.

RPR reactive at 1:64 with a reactive treponemal EIA. HIV antigen/antibody negative. Repeat gonorrhea and chlamydia NAAT negative. Urine hCG negative.

Impression: secondary syphilis. Prior gonococcal cervicitis, cleared.

Plan: benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM, single dose, given before she left; observed 30 minutes, no reaction. Counseled about a possible flu-like reaction in the first day. Reported to the health department, whose partner services staff will contact her. Quantitative RPR at 6 and 12 months; we are happy for her primary care office to follow the titers.

Sincerely,
Attending gynecologist

documents.title: ICU and hospital discharge summary (received 12/29/2025)
documents.author: pulmonary and critical care
documents.body:
Regional hospital, Pulmonary & Critical Care Medicine
Admitted 12/21/2025 via ED to MICU. Discharged 12/25/2025.
Patient: Jada Simmons  DOB 09/08/2001
Allergies: NKDA
PCP: copy to primary care

Principal diagnosis: status asthmaticus with impending respiratory failure
Other: severe persistent asthma; allergic rhinitis; pneumonia treated last month; gonococcal cervicitis and secondary syphilis, both treated

Presentation: 24 yo woman with severe persistent asthma, a prior intubation for asthma about two years ago, and recent pneumonia, with a week of steadily worse breathing despite using her albuterol more and more. On arrival RR 28, SpO2 89% on room air, using accessory muscles, able to say only a few words at a time. Peak flow 40% of her personal best. ABG: pH 7.32 / PaCO2 50 / PaO2 60 / HCO3 26.

Home medications on admission: albuterol HFA prn, fluticasone propionate HFA 220 mcg 1 puff BID (adherence inconsistent by her account), levocetirizine 5 mg prn.

ICU course: continuous nebulized albuterol with ipratropium, IV methylprednisolone, IV magnesium sulfate 2 g. Placed on BiPAP for about 24 hours with improvement in work of breathing and gas exchange; intubation was not needed. Portable chest film without consolidation or pneumothorax. Weaned off BiPAP, transferred to the medical floor on hospital day 3, nebulizers spaced, steroids changed to oral.

Discharge medications:
- prednisone 40 mg daily through 12/27 (5 days total of oral steroid)
- fluticasone propionate/salmeterol 250/50 mcg, 1 inhalation twice daily (NEW, replaces fluticasone HFA)
- albuterol HFA 2 puffs q4-6h prn
- levocetirizine 5 mg daily prn
STOP: fluticasone propionate HFA 220 mcg

Follow-up: PCP within 1 week; outpatient pulmonology referral recommended.
Inhaler technique taught by respiratory therapy before discharge.
Discharging physician: pulmonary/critical care attending

documents.title: Post-ICU Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Seen 5 days after discharge from the MICU (12/21-12/25), status asthmaticus, BiPAP, not intubated this time. Summary reviewed with her.

S: Much better. Finished prednisone 12/27. Albuterol once a day, no night waking since home. Using the new fluticasone-salmeterol disk twice a day; RT taught her in the hospital. Was able to fill it with the discount card. Cough from November gone.
O: comfortable, full sentences. Lungs clear, no wheeze, no crackles at the right base now. Heart regular.
A/P
1. Severe persistent asthma, two life-threatening exacerbations in two years. Now on ICS-LABA, which is where she should be. Teach-back on the disk inhaler done. Albuterol prn. Pulmonology referral sent as the hospital advised.
2. Pneumonia: resolved clinically and on the hospital film.
3. Gave her a written action plan for now; pulm will refine.
Return 2-3 months, sooner prn.

documents.title: Pulmonology consultation (received 02/16/2026)
documents.author: pulmonology
documents.body:
Outside pulmonary group
Date of consultation: 02/11/2026
Re: Jada Simmons, DOB 09/08/2001
Referred by: primary care
Allergies: NKDA

Thank you for asking me to see Ms. Simmons, a 24-year-old restaurant server with lifelong asthma. She was intubated for an exacerbation in January 2024 and spent part of a December 2025 admission in the ICU on BiPAP for status asthmaticus, a few weeks after a right lower lobe pneumonia. She has never smoked. Her mother has asthma.

Until December she was on fluticasone 220 mcg alone and by her own account used it about half the time. Since discharge she has been on fluticasone-salmeterol 250/50 twice daily and says she has missed only a handful of doses. Albuterol a few times a week, no night waking, no further steroid courses.

Exam: comfortable, conversant. No nasal polyps. Chest clear with a normal expiratory phase. No clubbing or edema.

Assessment: severe persistent asthma with two life-threatening exacerbations, better controlled now that she is on and actually using an ICS-LABA. Allergic rhinitis contributes in the spring and fall.

Recommendations:
1. Continue fluticasone-salmeterol 250/50 one inhalation twice daily; albuterol as needed.
2. Inhaler technique checked, good. Written asthma action plan reviewed and given.
3. Continue levocetirizine in pollen season.
4. I will see her again in about four months.

Thank you for involving me in her care.
Pulmonology attending
